_Knowledge: A Human Interest Story_ starts with the the following tetralemma, much like most arguments for interest-relativity in epistemology since @FantlMcGrath2022 have started. In the tetralemma, assume $p$ is some ordinary true proposition that we have tons of good, non-misleading evidence for, and which it is possible to truly believe on the basis of this good, non-misleading evidence, and $B$ is a bet that if accepted leads to a good result if $p$, and a bad result if $\neg p$.

1. It's possible to know that $p$.
2. If it's possible to know that $p$, then it's possible to know that $p$ while considering whether to accept $B$.
3. If one knows that $p$ while considering whether to accept $B$, then it is rationally permissible to accept $B$.
4. If the bad consequence of accepting $B$ if $\not p$ is bad enough, or the good consequence of accepting $B$ if $p$ is weak enough, and the grounds for $p$ are not completely conclusive, it is not rationally permissible to accept $B$.

Fill this in with various values of $B$ and $p$, and all four claims can seem almost trivial. Yet between them they imply that it both is and is not rationally permissible to accept $B$. So something has to give.

The book starts by setting out the four obvious responses to this tetralemma; denying in turn each of the four prongs. The _sceptic_ says that the first is false; in fact we don't know everyday propositions. What I call the _epistemicist_ denies the fourth. If one knows something, it has probability 1, so it is rational to take any bet on it. Now perhaps, they can add, taking $B$ is unwise, or reveals some other character flaw or bad disposition, but the acceptance itself is irrational. What I call the _orthodox_ view rejects 3. Now you might think this is a bad name for the rejection of 3, since few people go around explicitly denying 3. But most people in epistemology accept 1, 2, and 4, so they are committed to the denial of 3. The _pragmatist_, and the point of the book is to defend pragmatism, thinks that 3, and generalisations of it, are core to why knowledge matters, so they should be kept. Since 1 and 4 seem beyond dispute, the problem must be 2. Sometimes, being offered a bet means you cease to know that the bet is a winner. The particular kind of pragmatism I endorse is interest-relativity; what you know is a function of what you're interested in. So from now on I'll say that the view I endorse is interest-relativity.

The interest-relativist, as such, is completely neutral on contextualism. Sometimes, interest-relativism is taken to be very similar to contextualism; it is a 'shifty' view, and contextualism is another shifty view [@FantlMcGrath2012]. On the other hand, sometimes interest-relativism is motivated by problems for contextualism [@Stanley2005]. In the book, I don't take a stance on this debate. The tetralemma can, I think, be stated within a single context without making any premise less plausible, so just positing contextualism doesn't solve it. But neither does interest-relativism rule out contextualism. Despite their common origins in fin-de-siecle epistemology, interest-relativism and contextualism are just different views.

The orginal statements of interest-relativism in the 2000s focussed on cases where accepting $B$ led to huge losses if $\neg p$. So there came to be an assumption in the literature that the interest-relativist agreed with orthodoxy on everything except 'high stakes' cases. That isn't part of the view I defend in the book. If the gains from betting on $B$ and being right are small enough, and the book describes ways to make them arbitrarily small, the interest-relativist says that one can lose knowledge even if the potential losses are relatively modest. The main example in the book involves someone who might lose (in fact fail to gain) \$50 if they make an inadvisable bet. That turns out to be a high-enough stakes, largely because the gains are designed to be microscopic.

In Jason Stanley's version of interest-relativism, it was important that something _practical_ was at stake for interests to make a difference. That's there in the title of his book: _Knowledge and Practical Interests_. Following @FantlMcGrath2009, I don't think that's so. If one is idly wondering whether it would be a good idea to accept $B$, if one takes an _interest_ in it, that can be enough to trigger a change of knowledge states.
